# Intrinsic parity midpoint repair with variable capacities

This note applies the audited mixed-fiber selection theorem to an OLD
integer-midpoint coupling. It proves a full repair theorem, including
intrinsic lower-dimensional measure, exact preservation of parity
submarginals, optional marked source rows, pointwise capacities, and a
sharper degeneracy bound. It does not assert an OC center or infer
halfspace order from convex order.

## 1. Intrinsic setting and basic repair theorem

Let C be a convex body in R^n times R^d, let

    S=C intersect (Z^n times R^d),  S nonempty,
    q=dim_H S,   mu=H_q restricted to S.

Since S has finitely many nonempty compact convex fibers, q is their
maximum affine dimension. The measure mu is the sum of q-dimensional
Euclidean measure on its q-dimensional fibers; fibers of smaller
dimension have zero mu measure. For q=0, mu is counting measure on the
finite set S. In all cases 0<mu(S)<infinity.

Let gamma_-,gamma_+ be compactly supported finite measures of equal mass
M with gamma_-,gamma_+<=mu. Let Xi_old be a coupling of them such that

    (w_-+w_+)/2 belongs to S     Xi_old-almost everywhere.

Write rho_old for its midpoint law. There exists another coupling Xi
of the SAME gamma_-,gamma_+ whose midpoint law rho satisfies

    support rho subset S,
    rho_old<=_cx rho,
    rho<=2^n mu.                                  (1)

Here convex order uses every finite convex function in the full physical
ambient space. The new law uses one coupling for all these functions and
all subsequent halfspaces.

The repair preserves the input marginals separately within each common
parity class. More precisely, for r in (Z/2Z)^n set

    gamma_(i,r)=gamma_i restricted to bases congruent to r,
    M_r=gamma_(minus,r)(S)=gamma_(plus,r)(S).

The equality follows from the assumed integer midpoint of every old pair.
The coupling Xi is the sum of couplings Xi_r of these exact submarginals,
and its midpoint laws obey

    rho_old,r<=_cx rho_r,    rho_r<=mu,
    rho=sum_r rho_r.                              (2)

Joint masses assigned to individual ordered base pairs need not remain
fixed. That extra constraint is not asserted.

## 2. Why intrinsic degeneracy does not require global parallel fibers

Fix a parity class r with M_r>0. Every input fiber carrying positive
gamma_(i,r) mass has affine dimension q. In q>0 this follows from
absolute continuity with respect to mu; a positive-measure subset of a
q-dimensional affine space has full affine span there. In q=0 every
nonempty fiber is a singleton.

For q>0, take ANY positive-mass input fiber K_z from the minus side and
ANY such fiber K_w from the plus side. Their bases have common parity,
so p=(z+w)/2 is integer. Convexity gives

    (K_z+K_w)/2 subset K_p.

If L_z,L_w are their q-dimensional direction spaces, the affine dimension
of their Minkowski sum is dim(L_z+L_w). The target fiber has dimension
at most q by definition of q. Hence L_z=L_w. Comparing every cross pair
shows that ALL positive input fibers in this parity class share one
q-dimensional direction space L_r. Different parity classes may have
different direction spaces.

Choose orthogonal coordinates in L_r and L_r-perp. Write the affine hull
of each positive input fiber as b_z+L_r, where b_z lies in L_r-perp.
Regard (z,b_z) as a finite auxiliary base and the L_r coordinate as the
q-dimensional continuous variable. The mixed-fiber selection theorem
allows arbitrary finite real base sets, so these are legitimate auxiliary
coordinates. They are an orthogonal decomposition of the actual physical
space, not an asserted automorphism of the mixed-integer lattice.

Every product input pair in this parity class has an integer physical
base p and belongs to C after averaging. Its averaged fiber has positive
q-dimensional volume. It therefore lies in a q-dimensional target fiber
K_p, whose direction is L_r and whose perpendicular offset is necessarily

    b_p=(b_z+b_w)/2.

If two positive input pairs with the same p produced distinct such
offsets, K_p would contain two distinct parallel q-dimensional sets and
would have affine dimension at least q+1, impossible. Thus there is no
extra auxiliary-base multiplicity above a physical output fiber.

Apply mixed-fiber selection in these coordinates with continuous
dimension q and unit density ceilings. Its selected law is bounded by
q-dimensional Euclidean measure on each auxiliary output fiber. On each
physical output fiber that is exactly mu, and all outputs belong to S.
Its convex-order statement transports unchanged under the orthogonal
coordinate identification. This proves (2) when q>0.

For q=0, use the actual finitely many physical points as auxiliary discrete
bases. The discrete version of selection gives output atom masses at most
one. Every product pair in the fixed original parity class has integer
midpoint and belongs to C, hence to S. This proves (2) with counting
measure. Summing the at most 2^n classes proves (1).

## 3. Preserving marked source rows and their parity allocations

The repair can retain more than unmarked marginals. Suppose the old tuple
measure also carries a mark s in a standard Borel source space. Its
conditional pair distributions may depend on s. The mark can include the
original source point of a physical martingale. It can also carry any
additional finite or Borel bookkeeping labels that are not themselves
required to remain conditional endpoint marginals.

For every r, the convex order in (2) gives a compact martingale kernel
from rho_old,r to rho_r. Retain the OLD joint law of (s,r,old midpoint),
then apply that martingale kernel to its old midpoint. Finally disintegrate
Xi_r over its new midpoint and draw a new endpoint pair from that kernel.
This is a measurable composition of Borel kernels. It gives:

* exactly the old joint distribution of source mark and parity class;
* exactly the original endpoint submarginals gamma_(minus,r),gamma_(plus,r);
* midpoint law rho_r;
* the identity

    E[new midpoint | s,r]=E[old midpoint | s,r].    (3)

To prove the last claim, the midpoint of the final drawn pair equals its
intermediate point, and the martingale's conditional mean given the old
midpoint is that old midpoint. Apply the tower property. The assertion
does not require a separate repair chosen for each source row.

Thus a paired branch in a larger physical martingale may be replaced by
this construction while retaining its source barycenter and its old
source-to-parity masses. Conditional endpoint kernels and conditional
individual endpoint means may change. Preserving those stronger objects
would generally prevent density repair.

## 4. Stronger fiber-dependent and pointwise capacities

Let E_i=supp gamma_i and E_(i,r) its parity-r part. Define the compact
attainable midpoint set

    D_r=(E_(minus,r)+E_(plus,r))/2 subset S.

The repair can be chosen with

    rho_r<=1_(D_r) mu,
    rho<=kappa(w) mu,
    kappa(w)=number of active r with w in D_r.      (4)

This follows because every product pair used in the class repair belongs
to the displayed support sets. In particular it improves the global
2^n wherever not all parity classes can reach the same physical point.

There is a genuinely stronger version using varying input density
ceilings. Suppose bounded nonnegative upper-semicontinuous functions
a_i on the compact E_i satisfy gamma_i<=a_i mu. For t,s>=0 define

    H_q(t,s)=[(t^(-1/q)+s^(-1/q))/2]^(-q), q>=1,
    H_0(t,s)=min(t,s),

with H_q=0 if either argument is zero. For each parity class set

    c_r(w)=sup { H_q(a_-(u),a_+(v)):
                 u in E_(minus,r), v in E_(plus,r), (u+v)/2=w },     (5)

where the supremum of an empty set is zero. Then one can require

    rho_old,r<=_cx rho_r,
    rho_r<=c_r mu,
    rho<=sum_r c_r mu.                            (6)

Each c_r is bounded, compactly supported, and upper semicontinuous.
Indeed its defining pair set is compact, H_q is continuous and
coordinatewise nondecreasing on the nonnegative quadrant, and a convergent
sequence of maximizing pairs has a convergent subsequence above the
limiting midpoint. Consequently c_r mu is a well-defined finite measure.

Here is the additional density argument needed for (6). In the proof of
mixed-fiber selection, retain the density ceiling inside the weighted
area formula. For a smooth strongly convex surplus optimizer, its inverse
endpoint maps F_i on an output fiber and continuous derivatives T_i give

    h(w)<=a_i(F_i(w)) |det DT_i(w)|.

The common positive-semidefinite matrix identity from the audited slice
proof then gives, in continuous dimension q,

    h(w)<=H_q(a_-(F_-(w)),a_+(F_+(w)))<=c_r(w).

Zero ceilings cause no difficulty: the weighted area inequality makes
h zero at the relevant points. In q=0 endpoint determinism instead gives
the minimum of the endpoint atom ceilings, which is the same statement.

Thus every smooth strongly convex optimizer lies in the fixed class
{Xi:midpoint law<=c_r mu}. This class is convex and weakly closed on the
compact product. The smooth approximation, finite convex-test separation,
and compact finite-intersection argument applies verbatim and proves (6).
No separate optimizer for each final convex test remains in the result.

For a practical finite formula, take a_i constant on each positive input
fiber, with constants a_i(z), for instance its essential density supremum.
At an output base p, the capacity can be bounded by

    c_r(p,x)<=max_(z+w=2p, z,w congruent r)
                    H_q(a_-(z),a_+(w)),           (7)

with a maximum of zero if there is no such pair. Retaining in this maximum
only pairs whose actual continuous supports can average to x gives (5)
itself. This is a maximum within a parity class, not a sum over its base
pairs; the inverse endpoint maps are what avoid that extra multiplicity.

For unit ceilings, (5)-(6) reduce to (4). These are sufficient capacities;
no claim is made that (5) solves every further geometric optimization of
overlap among different parity classes.

## 5. A sharper bound when q<d

Let D be the projection of C onto R^n. When d>0 and p belongs to the
interior of D, the fiber C_p has nonempty interior in R^d. One proof is
to choose an interior point (p_0,x_0) of C, continue the segment from
p_0 through p slightly beyond p inside D, lift its farther endpoint to
C, and take the corresponding strict convex combination with a small
ambient ball about (p_0,x_0). Its fiber at p contains a d-dimensional
ball. Thus if q<d, every integer point of D lies on its boundary.

Fix any boundary output base p and a supporting hyperplane A of D at p.
If z,w in D have midpoint p, the supporting affine functional forces
z,w in A. The integer points in this affine hyperplane occupy at most
2^(n-1) parity classes. More precisely, if A meets Z^n, its integer
points form a coset of the lattice L=Z^n intersect direction(A), of
rank r<=n-1. The kernel of the map L->Z^n/2Z^n is exactly 2L: if
ell=2v belongs to L, then v is integer and lies in the same real
direction subspace. Thus the parity image has cardinality 2^r.

Consequently, at every physical point over p,

    kappa(p,x)<=2^r<=2^(n-1).                     (8)

For q<d this applies to every possible output base. Since n=0 would
force q=d for a convex body, the degenerate case has n>=1, and the
uniform intrinsic repair improves to

    rho<=2^(n-1) mu        when q<d.               (9)

For full-dimensional mixed measure, (8) remains an available local
improvement on boundary output bases. One may use a smaller affine
face containing all attainable endpoint bases to lower the rank further.

## 6. Exact sharpness, including intrinsic degeneracy

For full mixed dimension, let K be a d-dimensional convex body of volume
one, and take unit-density fibers at

    P_-={0,1}^n,    P_+={1,2}^n.

Both input measures have mass 2^n and lie in the convex body
[0,2]^n times K. An integer midpoint forces, coordinatewise,

    w=2*1-z,

so every output base is 1=(1,...,1). Its continuous coordinate remains
in K. Every integer-midpoint coupling therefore places mass 2^n in a
set of mixed volume one. The diagonal continuous pairing attains density
exactly 2^n. This proves that the uniform constant in (1) cannot be
improved even by a completely new admissible coupling. The same example
with K a point proves the counting statement for d=0.

The stronger degenerate constant (9) is also sharp. Let n>=1, 0<=q<d,
write x=(u,v) in R^q times R^(d-q), and choose 0<epsilon<1. Let K in
R^q have q-volume one, with K={0} and counting volume one if q=0. Define

    C={(z',t,u,v): z' in [0,2]^(n-1),
                    0<=t<=epsilon, u in K, |v|_infinity<=t}.

This is a full-dimensional convex body in R^n times R^d: choose t
strictly between zero and epsilon and strict inequalities in the other
nontrivial coordinates to get an interior point. Every integer base has
t=0, so every nonempty sampled fiber is K times {0} and dim_H S=q.

Use input bases {0,1}^(n-1) times {0} and {1,2}^(n-1) times {0}, each
with unit intrinsic density on its fiber. The same forced complement
pairing puts all mass 2^(n-1) in the single output fiber at base
(1,...,1,0), whose intrinsic measure is one. Its diagonal pairing attains
the ceiling exactly. This includes n=1, when the sharp ceiling is one,
and q=0, when all fiber measures are counting measures.

## 7. What affine ceilings help with, and what an affine tilt does not do

The variable-capacity theorem can preserve a nonconstant reference
density. Suppose a common bounded nonnegative function a on the relevant
physical set satisfies the midpoint condition

    a((u+v)/2)>=H_q(a(u),a(v))                     (10)

for the product pairs in a fixed parity class. If gamma_-,gamma_+<=a mu,
then (5) gives c_r<=a, so the repaired class law also obeys rho_r<=a mu.
For q>=1, any common log-concave a has (10), because

    H_q(a(u),a(v))<=sqrt(a(u)a(v))<=a((u+v)/2).

Nonnegative affine a satisfies it as well, by the arithmetic mean bound.
For q=0 use min(a(u),a(v)) in place of H_q. This is a theorem about the
ACTUAL input measures and their ACTUAL density ceilings, not permission
to tilt them without changing the coupling problem.

A tempting tilt shortcut fails even in an interval. Let gamma_-=gamma_+
be Lebesgue measure on [-1,1], and pair Y=-X. Then rho_old=2 delta_0.
Take the positive affine function a(x)=1+x/2. Tilting the old midpoint
law by a leaves it unchanged. But independently tilting each input
marginal gives a(x)dx; these still have mass two but have first moment
1/3. Every midpoint law of these tilted marginals therefore has first
moment 1/3, whereas a rho_old has first moment zero. They cannot stand
in convex order. Tilting a pair by a((X+Y)/2) does not induce the
individual tilted marginals a gamma_i.

Nor may one freely undo a tilt after obtaining convex order. For example

    delta_0 <=_cx (delta_(-1)+delta_1)/2.

Dividing the right side by 1+x/2 gives delta_(-1)+(1/3)delta_1, of mass
4/3 rather than one. Even after normalization its mean is -1/2, so it
does not dominate delta_0 in convex order. A perspective change of
coordinates would be a different construction requiring its own lattice
and measure proof.

Thus variable capacities and honest affine ceilings can improve a
particular instance. They do not remove the sharp uniform parity factor:
the examples of Section 6 force it for every admissible integer-midpoint
coupling, independently of the optimization or analytic test used.

## 8. Simultaneous cap credit and its exact present limit

For the selected tuple coupling, every closed ambient halfspace H obeys
the pointwise implication

    1_H(w_-)+1_H(w_+)>=1_H((w_-+w_+)/2).

It follows that

    gamma_-(H)+gamma_+(H)>=rho(H),                 (11)

simultaneously for every closed, possibly oblique H, with boundary mass
included. Classwise mass and the stronger capacities give

    rho_r(H)>= [M_r-integral_(S outside H)c_r dmu]_+,

and hence the numerical payment

    gamma_-(H)+gamma_+(H)
       >=sum_r [M_r-integral_(S outside H)c_r dmu]_+.                 (12)

The complement is strict because H is closed. This is a direct capacity
and tuple calculation, not an inference from convex order.

If the source carries supporting first-variation allocations rather
than literal halfspace indicators, (11)-(12) apply to those allocations
only after their equality with the literal traces is verified on these
measures. Density repair alone makes no new allocation identity.

Finally, rho need not have a mixed-integer centroid, uniform density,
log-concavity, or a deterministic point with a Grünbaum lower bound.
The old-to-new convex order is useful for rebuilding martingales via
Section 3, but it does not order source halfspace capture. Those are
separate steps in an OC proof. The new proven information here is the
intrinsic repair, its exact and locally refined capacities, its marked
row preservation, and its simultaneous endpoint cap payment.

This is a pending mathematical submission, not an accepted fact. Its definitions, scoped assertions, calculations, and limitations are given in the proposed argument below. A reference to another pending candidate supplies context only; it is not an accepted premise.

# Intrinsic parity midpoint repair with variable capacities

**Common intrinsic direction within a positive-mass parity class**

When q=dim_H S>0, all positive q-dimensional input fibers participating across one common integer parity class have a common q-dimensional direction space. Otherwise their Minkowski midpoint would have dimension greater than q in an actual integer fiber. Distinct auxiliary perpendicular output offsets likewise cannot coexist at one physical output base.

Scope limits: This concerns a common parity class of actual midpoint pairs; it is not a claim that all fibers of S are parallel.

**Parity repair preserves marked conditional midpoint means**

Classwise intrinsic density repair, followed by a compact martingale lift and disintegration, preserves both endpoint submarginals and every old marked-source/parity conditional midpoint mean. The repaired midpoint law dominates the old one in convex order and satisfies the classwise density ceiling.

Scope limits: Separate endpoint means within each marked row are not preserved. Convex order does not imply halfspace order or select an OC center. The source cites a compact martingale-existence dependency.

**Sharp full and degenerate parity density ceilings**

For unit-density endpoint inputs in the intrinsic parity repair, output density is bounded by the number of contributing parity classes: at most 2^n generally, and at most 2^(n-1) when q<d for a full ambient convex body. More locally the ceiling is 2^r for the rank r lattice in a supporting hyperplane. Forced-complement examples attain both uniform bounds, including q=0.

Scope limits: These are output-density capacities, not halfspace-depth constants. n=0 cannot have q<d under the full ambient-body hypothesis.
